analysis.one_liner: Would ban doctors from billing Medicare patients above capped charges and require refunds of excess fees.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor action in the 102nd Congress, dying in the House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce subcommittees after referral on April 28, 1992.
analysis.plain_summary: Non-participating Medicare doctors can bill patients above a legal cap, and patients often pay without knowing the extra charge is unenforceable. This bill would have made the cap binding—patients could not be held liable for excess charges—required refunds within 30 days, sanctioned doctors who repeatedly overbill, told beneficiaries about these rights in annual notices, and had Medicare's payment contractors check claims before paying to catch over-limit bills.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, especially seniors on fixed incomes who are billed above the legal limit by nonparticipating physicians and often pay it because they do not know the law caps their liability.

how_it_helps.text: Makes patients not liable for any charges a nonparticipating physician bills above the legal limiting charge for services on or after January 1, 1993.
Requires physicians to refund excess charges within 30 days of notice, or within 15 days after losing an appeal.
Authorizes sanctions against doctors who knowingly and repeatedly overbill or fail to refund on time.
Requires Medicare's annual notice to beneficiaries to explain they cannot be billed above the limiting charge and can get refunds.
Requires Medicare carriers to screen nonparticipating physicians' claims before payment to catch over-limit charges.

analysis.who_pays: Nonparticipating physicians, who would lose their ability to collect charges above the legal limit and could face sanctions for repeat overbilling or late refunds; Medicare carriers would bear added screening costs.

drawbacks.text: The enforcement runs through Medicare carriers doing prepayment screening of every nonparticipating physician's claim, adding administrative work and cost to the program.

Doctors who exceed the limiting charge face sanctions for 'knowing and willful' violations, which physicians' groups could argue adds penalties to an already contested balance-billing regime and might push some doctors out of seeing Medicare patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protection is real and targeted: it closes a gap where a legal cap exists on paper but patients get billed above it anyway. The costs are administrative—more screening and enforcement work for carriers and more compliance burden on doctors—which are modest next to the sums seniors can be overcharged.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and then to their health subcommittees, where it sat with no hearings, markup, or vote until the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. John Rhodes introduced the bill on April 28, 1992, and it was referred the same day to the House Committees on Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means.

Within weeks it was sent to the Subcommittee on Health (Ways and Means) and the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment (Energy and Commerce), where no further action was recorded before the Congress ended January 3, 1993.
The bill drew only two cosponsors—one Republican and one Democrat.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nonparticipating physicians remain able to bill Medicare patients above the legal limiting charge without a federal refund mandate, and beneficiaries continue to bear those excess charges unless state law or later federal rules protect them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Physicians billing above the Medicare cap

industries.note: The bill would strip these doctors of the practical ability to collect charges above Medicare's limiting charge and add refund deadlines and sanctions. Their interest in keeping that billing practice runs directly against beneficiaries' pockets.

industries.industry: Medicare claims carriers (private insurers processing Medicare Part B)
industries.note: Prepayment screening of nonparticipating physicians' claims adds work and cost for the contractors that process Medicare payments, though it serves the program's purpose of protecting beneficiaries.
